options.B: AWS Budgets with an alert threshold

explanation: B. Budgets watches spend (or usage) against thresholds you set and notifies — or triggers actions — when crossed. Cost Explorer (A) analyzes past spend but doesn't alert; the Calculator (C) estimates future architectures. Note: Budgets alert; they don't automatically stop the spending.

question: A team is designing a new three-tier application and needs a monthly cost estimate before requesting budget approval. Which tool?

options.B: Cost Explorer

explanation: C. The Pricing Calculator estimates planned architectures — it's the "before" tool. Cost Explorer (B) needs historical data that doesn't exist yet; Budgets (A) monitor ongoing spend; Trusted Advisor (D) checks best practices, not prices. Before → Calculator.

question: A startup wants to launch an app without buying any servers, paying only for what the app actually uses. Which model fits?

options.B: OpEx — consumption-based cloud spending

explanation: B. No upfront hardware plus pay-for-use is the OpEx/consumption model — the cloud's core financial pitch. CapEx (A) and leasing (D) both involve acquiring assets; private cloud (C) is still dedicated infrastructure with upfront cost.

question: A hospital must keep patient records in its own data center but run analytics on Azure. Which deployment model is this?

options.B: Private cloud

explanation: C. On-premises systems plus Azure, working together, is hybrid by definition — often driven by regulation, latency, or legacy constraints. Azure Arc is Microsoft's hybrid-management story. Multi-cloud (D) would mean multiple public providers, which isn't described here.

question: A startup's web app idles overnight but spikes every weekday at noon. Under a consumption-based model, what happens to their cloud bill?

options.A: It stays flat — they pay the same every month
options.B: It tracks actual usage: near-zero overnight, higher at the noon spike — they pay for what they consume
options.C: They must prepay a year of peak capacity
options.D: Spikes are free; only baseline usage is metered

explanation: B. Consumption-based = metered like a utility: the bill follows real usage up and down. Idle resources cost ~nothing; the noon spike costs more — and scaling back down stops the meter. Flat fees (A) and upfront commitments (C) are the opposite pattern (commitments can discount consumption pricing, but the metering underneath stays).

question: Under the shared responsibility model, who is responsible for the physical security of Azure data centers?

options.B: Microsoft — physical hosts and facilities are the provider's responsibility

explanation: B. Physical security of data centers, hosts, and the hypervisor is Microsoft's side of the line — always. The customer owns what's in the cloud: data, identities, configurations. "Who secures the building?" → the provider, on every cloud exam.

question: An auditor needs read-only visibility into all Azure resources but must not change anything. What is the correct assignment?

options.A: Owner role at the management group
options.B: Reader role at the subscription scope
options.C: Contributor role on each resource group
options.D: A CanNotDelete lock on the subscription

explanation: B. Reader = view everything, change nothing — exactly the requirement — and subscription scope covers all resource groups beneath it. Owner (A) is wildly excessive; Contributor (C) allows changes; a lock (D) blocks deletion but isn't an access grant at all.

question: The company requires every VM to carry an "Owner" tag and forbids VMs in regions outside the US. Which control enforces both?

options.A: RBAC — assign the Tag Contributor role
options.B: Resource locks on each VM
options.C: Azure Policy — tag requirements and allowed-location rules

explanation: C. Both requirements are about what resources may exist — Azure Policy's exact job, evaluated at deployment and continuously. RBAC (A) governs who acts; locks (B) block actions on specific resources; subscriptions (D) are billing boundaries, not rule engines.

question: A production database must be protected against accidental deletion, but administrators still need to modify its configuration. Which lock fits?

options.B: CanNotDelete — blocks deletion, allows modification
options.C: An Azure Policy denying all writes

explanation: B. CanNotDelete is precisely "you may change it, you may not destroy it." ReadOnly (A) would block the needed config changes. A policy (C) is the wrong tool for per-resource protection; removing RBAC (D) just breaks legitimate administration.

question: Before requesting budget for a new Azure deployment, the team needs a monthly cost projection. Which tool?

options.B: The Pricing Calculator — estimate planned costs

explanation: B. The Pricing Calculator is the "before" tool: model the planned architecture, get a monthly estimate. Cost Management (A) and Advisor (C) analyze existing spend; Budgets (D) watch ongoing thresholds. Before → Calculator, every time.

question: An attacker alters prices in an online store's database. Customers are charged wrong amounts, but no data was stolen and the site stayed up. Which security goal was violated?

options.B: Integrity

explanation: B. The data was altered without authorization — the textbook integrity violation. Nothing was exposed (not confidentiality) and the site worked fine (not availability). Non-repudiation (D) is about proving who did something, which isn't the issue here.

question: A company has no firewall and an unpatched web server, but operates on an isolated network with no external connectivity and no malicious insiders. What best describes its risk from internet attackers?

options.B: Low — with no threat able to reach the vulnerabilities, that risk pairing doesn't exist
options.C: Zero — air gaps eliminate all risk

explanation: B. Risk needs both threat and vulnerability. Severe vulnerabilities (A) with no reachable threat produce little risk from that threat. But "zero" (C) overreaches — insider threats, USB drops, and supply-chain issues remain. Risk is always threat × vulnerability × impact.

question: A bank requires two employees to jointly authorize any wire transfer over $10,000. Which principle is this?

options.B: Defense in depth

explanation: C. Splitting a critical action so no single person can complete it alone is separation of duties — the classic fraud control. Least privilege (A) is about how much access each person has, not about splitting one action between two people.

question: A hospital can't patch an MRI workstation (the vendor forbids it), so it isolates the machine on its own VLAN with extra monitoring. What kind of control is the isolation?

options.B: Deterrent — it discourages attackers
options.C: Compensating — a substitute where the primary control can't be applied

explanation: C. Patching (the primary control) is impossible, so isolation + monitoring compensates — it doesn't fix the vulnerability (not corrective), it substitutes protection around it. Compensating controls are the exam's answer whenever "we can't do the normal thing, so we do this instead."

question: A company’s email system has an RTO of 4 hours and an RPO of 1 hour. What do these require?

options.B: Restore within 4 hours of an outage, and lose no more than 1 hour of email data — which means hourly (or better) backups
options.C: Backups every 4 hours, restore within 1 hour
options.D: Four hours of downtime per week is acceptable

explanation: B. RTO is the downtime allowance (back within 4h); RPO is the data-loss allowance (≤1h behind → backups at least hourly). Swapping them (C) is the classic confusion — read which letter is which: T=time down, P=point (data) behind.
domain: Business Continuity, Disaster Recovery & Incident Response

question: Before writing its disaster recovery plan, a company analyzes which business processes are critical and what downtime costs per hour. What is this analysis called?

options.B: A business impact analysis (BIA)

explanation: B. The BIA identifies critical processes and quantifies impact — and it comes before the BCP/DRP, because the plans' RTO/RPO targets derive from it. You can't plan recovery sensibly without knowing what matters most and what it costs to lose.
domain: Business Continuity, Disaster Recovery & Incident Response

question: A trading firm needs failover within minutes of a site loss, cost is secondary. Which recovery site type fits?

options.B: Hot site — fully equipped and ready, failover in minutes

explanation: B. Hot = ready now (minutes), warm = hours, cold = days. The RTO (minutes) selects the site type; the budget just has to accept it. Backups alone (D) restore data, not a running site — recovery needs both.
domain: Business Continuity, Disaster Recovery & Incident Response

question: During a suspected breach, the team isolates affected hosts before investigating the cause. Which incident response phase is this, and why this order?

options.B: Containment — stop the spread first; investigating an uncontained incident lets damage continue

explanation: B. Containment comes before deep investigation: you stop the bleeding, then diagnose. Investigating first while the attacker keeps moving is analysis during an active fire. (And containment preserves evidence — unlike wiping, which destroys it.)
domain: Business Continuity, Disaster Recovery & Incident Response

question: During an active ransomware outbreak, the IR team debates whether to immediately wipe infected machines or isolate them from the network first. What is the correct order and why?

options.A: Wipe first — eradication before containment saves time
options.B: Isolate (contain) first — stop the spread before removing the cause
options.C: Recover from backup first, then investigate
options.D: Skip to post-incident review to save time

explanation: B. Containment comes before eradication: isolating hosts stops ransomware from reaching new victims while you work. Wiping first (A) destroys forensic evidence and doesn't stop the still-spreading infection elsewhere. The phase order exists because each step protects the next.

question: An analyst needs to preserve evidence from a running compromised server. Following the order of volatility, what should be captured first?

options.A: The disk image — it holds the most data
options.B: System logs from last week
options.C: RAM contents — the most volatile evidence

explanation: C. Order of volatility: capture the most ephemeral first. RAM (running processes, encryption keys, network connections) vanishes when power dies; disk and logs persist. Imaging the disk first (A) is fine after RAM — but RAM can't wait.

question: A SOC receives 10,000 IDS alerts per day and analysts have started ignoring the queue. What is the underlying problem and the fix?

options.A: Too few analysts — hire more Tier 1 staff
options.B: Alert fatigue from untuned detections — tune rules to cut false positives
options.C: The IDS is misplaced — move it behind the firewall

explanation: B. This is textbook alert fatigue: noisy, low-fidelity detections train humans to ignore all alerts — including the real ones. The fix is tuning (better rules, correlation, prioritization), not more eyeballs on the same noise. Detection quality is an operations discipline.

question: After containing a breach, what must happen before affected systems return to production?

options.A: Nothing — containment is the last step
options.B: Eradication of the root cause and verification the systems are clean
options.D: Deleting all logs to save disk space

explanation: B. The phase order is contain → eradicate → recover. Returning still-compromised systems to production re-infects the environment and wastes the containment effort. Eradication (remove malware, close the entry point, reset compromised credentials) plus verification comes first — recovery is the reward for clean systems.

question: A shared project directory must let team members create files, but every new file should belong to the project group automatically. Which mechanism does this?

options.A: Setting the setgid bit on the directory
options.B: Setting the sticky bit on the directory
options.D: Making every user the directory owner

explanation: A. setgid on a directory makes new files inherit the directory's group instead of the creator's primary group — the standard shared-folder pattern. The sticky bit (B) controls deletion (only your own files); 777 (C) is a security disaster, not a group strategy.

question: A web service is configured to run as its own dedicated user account with no login shell, instead of as root. Why?

options.A: To make the service start faster
options.B: Least privilege — a compromised service shouldn't hand over root
options.D: Because root cannot run network services

explanation: B. A service running as root that gets exploited gives the attacker root. A dedicated unprivileged user contains the blast radius — the process can only touch what that user may touch. That's least privilege applied to daemons, and it's why service users exist.

question: A file has permissions 640. Which statement is true?

options.B: The owner can read and write; the group can read; others have no access
options.C: The group can write but not read
options.D: The owner has full control including execute

explanation: B. Decode: 6 = rw- (owner: read+write), 4 = r-- (group: read), 0 = --- (other: nothing). It's the classic "my group can read my work, the world can't" setting — common for config files with secrets readable by a service group.

question: An administrator wants users to run only the backup script as root, without knowing the root password. Which tool and concept is this?

options.A: su — switching to the root account entirely
options.B: sudo — delegated, audited privilege for specific commands
options.D: chown — giving users ownership of the script

explanation: B. sudo grants specific commands as root (configured in sudoers), logging each use — delegation without sharing the password. su (A) hands over a full root shell (all-or-nothing); chmod/chown (C, D) change file permissions, not user privilege. "Specific commands as root, no password sharing" → sudo.

question: A script must back up a database every night at 2:30 AM. Which cron entry is correct?

options.B: 2 30 * * * /usr/local/bin/db-backup.sh

explanation: A. Cron fields are minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week: 30 minutes past 2 AM, every day = 30 2 * * *. (B) swaps minute and hour (2:30 AM vs. 30:02 — invalid); (C) and (D) put the numbers in the wrong fields entirely. Read left to right, five fields.

question: Inside double quotes, "$HOME" expands to the home directory. Inside single quotes it stays literal. What is this distinction called, and why does it matter?

options.B: Quoting — it controls whether the shell interprets special characters

explanation: B. Quoting controls interpretation: double quotes allow $ expansion; single quotes suppress it. Scripts break mysteriously when a variable that should expand doesn't (or vice versa) — this is the #1 beginner scripting bug — verify your quoting.

question: A deployment script must be safe to run twice in a row without duplicating its effects. What property is this?

options.B: Idempotence

explanation: B. Idempotence: running it N times has the same effect as running it once. Schedules overlap, playbooks re-run, humans double-click — automation that isn't idempotent eventually corrupts state. It's the defining property of reliable configuration management.

question: A company manages 200 web servers and wants the same Apache configuration enforced on all of them automatically. Which approach fits?

options.A: SSH into each server and edit the config by hand
options.B: A configuration management tool declaring the desired state
options.C: A cron job that emails the admin daily

explanation: B. Declared desired state, enforced everywhere identically and continuously — that's configuration management (Ansible/Puppet/Chef). Manual edits (A) guarantee drift across 200 machines; cron emails (C) only report; the goal is enforcement, not notification.

question: A defense contractor's system enforces that analysts cleared to Secret cannot read Top Secret documents. Which model is this?

options.B: Bell-LaPadula

explanation: B. Government classification + confidentiality + "no read up" = Bell-LaPadula, the confidentiality model built for exactly this. Biba (A) is the integrity mirror; Clark-Wilson (C) is commercial-transaction integrity; Brewer-Nash (D) handles conflicts of interest (consultants vs. competing clients).

question: A single loss expectancy of $100,000 with an annualized rate of occurrence of 0.5 gives what ALE, and what does it mean?

options.A: $200,000 — the cost of eliminating the risk
options.B: $50,000 — the expected yearly loss, used to justify control spending

explanation: B. ALE = SLE × ARO = $100,000 × 0.5 = $50,000/year. It's the expected annual loss — the number that justifies control budgets: don't spend $200K/year to mitigate a $50K/year risk. It's a decision tool, not a premium quote (D).

question: An accounting system requires one employee to enter a payment and a different employee to approve it. Which concept is this, and which model formalizes it?

options.B: Separation of duties — Clark-Wilson

explanation: B. Splitting a transaction across two people so neither can complete fraud alone is separation of duties, and Clark-Wilson is the integrity model that formalizes it (well-formed transactions + SoD + auditing). Least privilege (A) limits how much access one person has — related but different.

question: After a flood destroys the primary data center, the company activates its alternate site and continues serving customers while IT rebuilds systems. Which plan governed the customer-facing continuation?

options.B: The business continuity plan (BCP)

explanation: B. Keeping the business serving customers from the alternate site is business continuity; the DRP covers restoring the technology (rebuilding systems). BCP = business keeps running; DRP = IT gets rebuilt. The scenario describes the former.

question: A company discovers a ten-year-old customer database nobody uses, stored unencrypted on a forgotten server. What is the core asset-security failure?

options.A: The data was never classified, so no retention or protection lifecycle applied
options.B: The server hardware is too old
options.D: The company needs a bigger firewall

explanation: A. Unclassified data gets no lifecycle: no retention schedule (so it was never destroyed), no protection requirements (so it sat unencrypted). Classification at creation would have assigned both. The hardware age (B) and firewall (D) miss the point — this is a governance-of-data failure.

question: An SSD containing restricted data is being retired. The team destroys the encryption keys, rendering all data on the drive unrecoverable. What is this called?

options.B: Overwriting

explanation: C. Destroying the keys so ciphertext can never be decrypted is cryptographic erasure — fast, verifiable, and ideal for SSDs where overwriting can't reliably reach every cell (wear-leveling hides blocks). Degaussing (A) doesn't work on flash media; formatting (D) is not destruction.

question: A backup tape is stolen from a courier van. The backups were encrypted with AES-256. Which data state was protected, and what is the exposure?

options.A: Data in transit was protected; exposure is minimal if key management was sound
options.B: Data at rest was protected; the thieves can read everything
options.D: Data in use was protected; the tapes are unreadable

explanation: A. A backup tape in a van is data in transit (moving between locations), and the encryption protected exactly that state. With sound key management, the thieves hold unreadable ciphertext. This is why backup encryption exists — media gets lost; encryption makes loss survivable.

question: A privacy review finds the app collects location data "just in case" with no defined purpose or deletion schedule. Which principle is violated?

options.B: Data minimization and purpose limitation

explanation: B. Collecting data without purpose and keeping it indefinitely violates minimization (collect only what you need) and purpose limitation (use it only for the stated purpose). "Just in case" data is breach liability with no business value — and under GDPR, it's unlawful.

question: A developer builds database queries by concatenating user input directly into SQL strings. What vulnerability is this, and what is the fix?

options.B: SQL injection — use parameterized queries / prepared statements

explanation: B. Concatenated input executed as SQL is the textbook SQL injection pattern. The fix is structural: parameterized queries separate code from data so input can never become instructions. Output encoding (A) fixes XSS, a different bug in a different place.

question: A security team wants to find vulnerabilities in a running staging application, testing it the way an attacker would. Which method fits?

options.B: DAST — dynamic testing of the running app from outside

explanation: B. Running app + external attacker perspective = DAST. SAST (A) needs source code and doesn't see runtime behavior; linters (C) check style, not security; unit tests (D) verify intended behavior, not resistance to malicious input.

question: An audit finds the production web server still uses the vendor's default admin password. Which OWASP category is this?

options.B: Cryptographic failures

explanation: C. Default credentials are the poster child of security misconfiguration: the software is fine, the deployment is negligent. It's not an injection flaw (A) or a crypto failure (B) — it's "we never finished setting it up." Misconfiguration is consistently a top-10 finding because it's so common.

question: Why does the CISSP emphasize finding vulnerabilities during design rather than after deployment?

options.B: Fixing earlier is dramatically cheaper — "shift left"

explanation: B. The cost curve is brutal: a flaw caught in design costs a conversation; the same flaw in production costs emergency patches, downtime, and possibly breach notification. "Shift left" is the economic argument for threat modeling and secure design — spend a little early to avoid spending a fortune late.

question: A team runs a web API that must survive pod failures and update without downtime. Which controller fits, and why?

options.A: Job — it runs the API to completion
options.B: Deployment — maintains replicas and does rolling updates
options.C: DaemonSet — one API pod per node

explanation: B. Deployments maintain the declared replica count through failures (self-healing) and roll out new versions gradually (rolling updates) with rollback available. Jobs (A) terminate; DaemonSets (C) are for node agents, not scaled APIs; bare pods (D) are never rescheduled when they die.

question: A pod is running but a dependent cache isn't ready, so the pod shouldn't receive traffic yet. Which probe controls this?

options.A: Liveness — it will restart the pod
options.B: Readiness — it controls whether the pod gets traffic
options.C: Startup — it delays all other probes

explanation: B. Readiness gates traffic: failing readiness removes the pod from service endpoints without restarting it. Liveness (A) would restart a merely-unready pod — the classic misconfiguration that turns a slow dependency into a crash loop. Alive ≠ ready.

question: A pod specifies CPU request 500m and limit 1000m. What do these mean?

options.B: The scheduler guarantees 500m; the pod is throttled if it tries to exceed 1000m
options.C: It can use 1000m only on weekends
options.D: Requests and limits must be equal

explanation: B. Requests are the scheduling guarantee (the scheduler only places the pod where 500m is free); limits are the enforcement ceiling (CPU throttling beyond 1000m; memory beyond limit → OOM kill). Requests drive placement; limits drive runtime enforcement.

question: Traffic to an API doubles every weekday morning. Which autoscaler adds more pod replicas based on CPU?

options.B: Cluster autoscaler

explanation: C. HPA scales replicas (horizontal) on metrics like CPU — more pods for more traffic. VPA (A) resizes requests/limits (vertical); the cluster autoscaler (B) adds nodes; CronJobs (D) run scheduled tasks. "More pods" → horizontal → HPA.

question: A developer's pod needs 10Gi of storage that survives pod restarts and is created automatically when requested. Which objects are involved?

options.B: A PVC requesting 10Gi, fulfilled by dynamic provisioning via a StorageClass

explanation: B. The developer writes a PVC (the request); a StorageClass dynamically provisions the PV — no admin pre-creation, survives pod death. hostPath (A) ties the pod to one node; emptyDir (C) dies with the pod; ConfigMaps (D) hold config, not 10Gi of data.

question: A database pod was deleted and recreated, but its data is gone. The pod used an emptyDir volume. What went wrong?

options.A: emptyDir survives pod deletion — this is a scheduler bug
options.B: emptyDir only survives container restarts; pod deletion wipes it — persistent data needs a PV/PVC
options.C: The database should have used a ConfigMap

explanation: B. emptyDir's lifetime is the pod, not the container: it survives container crashes (useful scratch space) but dies with the pod. Durable data needs a PersistentVolumeClaim. This is the #1 storage misconception — always verify the volume type.

question: A shared media library must be mounted read-write by pods on many nodes simultaneously. Which access mode is required?

options.B: ReadOnlyMany (ROX)
options.D: Access modes don't matter for shared data

explanation: C. Many nodes × read-write = ReadWriteMany. RWO (A) allows one node; ROX (B) is read-only. And the backend must actually support RWX (NFS/CephFS do; plain block storage doesn't) — a PVC asking for RWX on an RWO-only provisioner pends forever.

question: A PVC is deleted and the admin wants the underlying data preserved for manual review. Which reclaim policy should the PV use?

options.B: Retain — keeps the PV and its data for manual handling
options.D: Reclaim policies only apply to ConfigMaps

explanation: B. Retain keeps the PV and its data after the claim is gone — the admin then inspects, backs up, or manually cleans up. Delete (A) would destroy the very data to be reviewed. Retain is the safe default when data matters more than automation.

question: An application needs its logs shipped to a central system, but the app itself can't be modified. Which pod design fits?

options.A: An init container that ships logs then exits
options.B: A sidecar container sharing the pod's volumes that tails and ships the logs
options.C: A second Deployment for the logging agent
options.D: A CronJob that restarts the app hourly

explanation: B. The sidecar pattern exists for exactly this: a helper container sharing the pod's network/volumes, running alongside the unmodifiable main container. Init containers (A) exit before the app starts — they can't ship ongoing logs. A separate Deployment (C) can't see the pod's local log files.

question: A database migration must run to completion before the application starts, and must block startup if it fails. Which construct?

options.B: An init container — runs to completion before app containers start
options.D: A second replica of the app

explanation: B. Init containers run sequentially to completion before any app container starts — and a failed init container blocks the pod. That's the "migrate first, then start" gate. Sidecars (A) run alongside; probes (C) check running containers; replicas (D) don't order anything.

question: A team's production incident was caused by ":latest" resolving to a different image than tested. What is the robust fix?

options.B: Pin images by digest (@sha256:…) so deployments reference exact bits

explanation: B. Tags are mutable — :latest today isn't :latest tomorrow. Digests pin the exact image bits, making deployments reproducible: what you tested is what you ship. Pulling more often (A) makes the drift worse, not better.

question: A nightly report job occasionally fails from transient network errors and must retry automatically. Which Kubernetes behavior handles this, and what must the job guarantee?

options.A: Deployments restart it; the job must be stateless
options.B: The Job controller retries failed pods (backoffLimit); the work must be idempotent
options.C: CronJobs never retry; the job must never fail
options.D: The scheduler retries; the job must be faster

explanation: B. Jobs exist for run-to-completion work and retry failures automatically — but retries are only safe if the work is idempotent (re-running doesn't duplicate effects). A non-idempotent job retried by the platform is a data-corruption machine. Design for retry.

question: Pods behind a service keep getting replaced, but clients never change their configuration. What makes this possible?

options.B: The service provides a stable virtual IP + DNS name selecting pods by label

explanation: B. That's the service's entire job: a stable front (ClusterIP + DNS name) over a changing set of backends, tracked via label selectors and endpoints. Clients point at the service; Kubernetes handles the churn behind it. Pod IPs (A) are explicitly ephemeral.

question: A team runs 12 HTTP microservices and wants one public entry point routing by URL path, with TLS termination. Which construct?

options.B: Ingress — one entry point, L7 host/path routing, TLS termination

explanation: B. Ingress is the L7 front door: one load balancer, routing by host/path to backend services, commonly terminating TLS. Twelve LoadBalancers (A) means twelve cloud bills; NodePorts (C) expose awkward high ports with no path routing; headless (D) is for direct pod access, the opposite need.

question: After applying a NetworkPolicy that selects all pods in a namespace but defines no ingress rules, what happens to pod-to-pod traffic?

options.B: All ingress to selected pods is denied (default-deny)
options.C: All traffic is allowed as before

explanation: B. Selecting pods with a policy makes them isolated for the specified direction; with no ingress rules, nothing is allowed in — default deny. That's the intended hardening pattern: deny all, then add explicit allow-policies. (DNS commonly needs an explicit egress exception — a classic follow-up bug.)

question: A service exists but curl to its ClusterIP times out. The fastest diagnostic check is:

options.B: Check the service's endpoints — empty means the selector matches no pods

explanation: B. "Service exists, nothing answers" is almost always a selector mismatch: the service selects by labels, and if no pods carry those labels, the endpoints list is empty. Checking endpoints takes seconds and confirms it. The other options treat symptoms blindly.

question: An app takes 90 seconds to warm its cache, but the liveness probe kills it at 30 seconds every time. What is the correct fix?

options.B: Add a startup probe giving the app its warm-up window before liveness begins

explanation: B. The startup probe exists for exactly this: it gates liveness/readiness until initialization completes, so slow starters aren't murdered mid-boot. Removing probes (A) blinds the platform; readiness (C) doesn't affect liveness killing; replicas (D) just multiply the crash loop.

question: A pod shows CrashLoopBackOff and its events mention OOMKilled. What happened and what is the fix?

options.A: The node ran out of disk — clean the node
options.B: The container exceeded its memory limit and was killed — raise the memory limit (or fix the leak)
options.C: The image is corrupted — rebuild it
options.D: The scheduler is broken — restart it

explanation: B. OOMKilled = the kernel killed the container for breaching its memory limit; CrashLoopBackOff = Kubernetes keeps retrying. The fix is a higher limit (if legitimate usage) or fixing the memory leak (if not). Disk (A) and image (C) produce different errors entirely.

question: During a rolling update, new pods start but get traffic before their caches warm, causing user-facing errors. Which probe misconfiguration is this?

options.B: Readiness isn't gating traffic until the pod is actually ready
options.C: Startup probes are forbidden during updates
options.D: Probes can't affect traffic at all

explanation: B. Readiness's job is exactly this: keep unready pods out of service endpoints. If new pods receive traffic while cold, readiness isn't checking real readiness (or isn't configured). Liveness (A) would restart them — a different failure mode.

question: An on-call engineer sees elevated error rates on one microservice but doesn't know which downstream call is failing. Which observability tool answers "which hop is slow/failing"?

options.A: Container logs on the frontend pod
options.B: Distributed tracing — following the request across services

explanation: B. One request crossing five services needs tracing: each hop timed and linked to the same trace ID, revealing exactly which downstream call fails or lags. Logs (A) show one service's view; node metrics (D) show infrastructure, not request paths.
